properties.Desc_: The area surrounding the Paracel Archipelago, contested by China and Vietnam, but under PRC control since 1974, it is an area of relatively intense human activity due to its many islands and proximity to the coasts of both claimants, which render it relatively accessible.
Relatively narrow stretch of shallow sea contested by China and Vietnam, and subject to a border demarcation agreement since 2000 that is not recognized by the ROC.

A much deeper area offshore from the largest Philippine island, Luzon, encompassing the Sino-Philippine bilaterally dispute over the large isolated atoll Scarborough Shoal, where Chinese, Vietnamese and Filipino fisherfolk have all traditionally operated
A stretch of relatively shallow waters on the continental shelf of central Vietnam, where energy explorations have shown promising oil and gas prospects.

An oil-rich area of the Vietnamese continental shelf extending some 400 kilometers from the country’s southern coast, mostly within the nine-dash line. Vietnam has built observation stations in several of shallower patches of water, and has numerous energy projects to full production via pipelines to the mainland.

The most contested area of the Spratly Archipelago, but also the most remote from any side’s coast. The area contains the Thitu Reefs, Tizard Bank and Union Reefs, where the PRC, Philippines and Vietnam all occupy numerous features. Taiwan also occupies the largest island there. The area is rich in fisheries but not believed to contain significant oil.

The area closest to the Philippine island of Palawan, featuring shallower waters and promising oil and gas reserves both at Reed Bank as well as relative proximity to the Philppine coast. Features here are almost all underwater reefs, claimed by the PRC and the Philippines.
A highly contested area with several small land features, most of which are controlled by Vietnam, with single features occupied by the PRC and Malaysia.

A generally deep, remote area littered with many dangerous, isolated atolls (but with abundant fisheries), most of which lie just below the waterline at high tide, and subject to claims by the PRC, Philippines, and Malaysia. Only the latter two countries occupy features in the area.

The remaining area at the far southern end of the nine-dash line area, north of Borneo, where the PRC’s nine-dash line overlaps with Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei’s EEZ and Continental Shelf claims. Very few features are occupied, Malaysia’s diving resort on Swallow Reef being a rare exception – but the area is rich in fish stocks as well as undersea oil and gas, which Malaysia has brought to production.
